newsitem.title: USA: N. Carolina beach residents return to wrecked homes.
newsitem.headline: N. Carolina beach residents return to wrecked homes.

text.p: Residents of Topsail Island returned to their homes Saturday for the first time since Hurricane Fran crushed North Carolina's tiny beach communities, to find littered streets, crumbled homes and belongings scattered far and wide.
Halted as they drove up to National Guard roadblocks, homeowners toted chainsaws and shovels along sand-coated beach roadways to begin the massive process of digging out.

On Topsail Island, northeast of Wilmington, dozens of expensive beachfront homes were undermined by Fran's powerful tidal surge and crumbled into the sea, or were swept off their foundations and dumped hundreds of feet away.
Other homes were smacked by 120-mph winds that tore off roofs, shattered windows and buckled walls when Hurricane Fran roared ashore in North Carolina Thursday evening.
Local officials said Surf City and Topsail Beach on the barrier island were perhaps the hardest hit of the beach towns.
"It was hell out here. The walls were buckling," said Tim Hallwas, 30, who rode out the storm in his wood-framed Surf City home. "I was talking to God. We became good friends."

By Saturday evening, almost 48 hours after Fran made landfall at Cape Fear in North Carolina, authorities had reported 21 dead in five states as a result of the storm, which remained a powerful weather system long after making landfall, causing serious flooding as it moved inland.
Most residents evacuated Surf City as Fran approached and were allowed to return only Saturday to see if their homes were still standing.
"I can't believe the destruction," said Surf City resident Tommy Oliver, 49. "Everybody's belongings are in the street."
"We lost a lot of our artwork," said Carolina Redding, 25, as she pulled a sand-spattered canvas from a waterlogged wood frame. "We found a lot of it over the other side of the island in the bushes."
Gloria and Rick Turner waded toward their beachfront dream home.
"I'm glad I took a little anxiety pill before I came here," said Gloria Turner, who with her husband built their home there in 1989. The front door stood wide open as they approached.

"Oh my lord. Oh my lord," she said as she worked through the house. Flood waters had ravaged the ground-floor garage carrying a freezer into the littered front yard, and ripped off a wood deck with an ocean view.

High winds had opened up the roof and rainwater collapsed part of the ceiling, littering the interior with pink fiberglass insulation. But the windows, much of the furniture and precious family pictures remained intact.
"Honey, this isn't too bad, is it?" Turner asked her husband, pronouncing herself "very relieved. When you see the people who don't have homes, I thank God."

One of the strangest sights on the upscale barrier island was its normally pristine beach, which was littered with thousands of car and truck tires as far as could be seen. Residents said the tires had been sunk offshore for artificial reefs several years ago and were dredged up by the storm.
